notes: Several architectural violations found. (1) Rule 1 broken: The router directly calls both taskSvc.get() and userSvc.get() to resolve taskTitle and authorName before calling commentSvc.create() — this is cross-service orchestration in the router, not via Event Bus. The comment.added event payload includes taskTitle and authorName, meaning the CommentService itself receives data from other services' domains through its create() signature, leaking cross-service knowledge. A cleaner design would have the NotificationService subscribe and look up needed data, or the TaskService/UserService publish richer events. (2) Rule 2 broken: CommentService.create() accepts taskTitle and authorName parameters sourced from other services' stores, meaning it depends on data owned by TaskService and UserService — violating exclusive data ownership. The router acts as a data broker between services. (3) The status transition validation allows same-status transitions (newIdx === oldIdx passes), which may or may not be intentional but is arguably a logic flaw for a 'forward-only' rule. (4) Notification logic for comment.added only notifies the author of the comment, not the task assignee or project members — this is semantically wrong (author already knows they commented). (5) The setImmediate async dispatch in EventBus means the demo's notification check may race against event processing — notifications may not appear in the GET response immediately after the triggering action, which the demo does not account for. (6) Error responses for invalid status transitions use res.writeHead(400) then res.end(e.message) which is correct, but the pattern res.writeHead(404) && res.end() is used throughout — writeHead returns the ServerResponse, which is truthy, so the short-circuit always evaluates res.end(), but this is a fragile/misleading pattern. (7) genId() using Math.random() has collision risk in production but is acceptable for demo. (8) No input validation (missing required fields, invalid types) in any service. (9) UpdateTaskInput intentionally excludes status/assigneeId (good), but the generic update() method on TaskService could be misused. (10) Types file is well-structured. Overall the architecture is recognizable but has meaningful violations of the stated rules, particularly around service isolation and event-bus-only communication.
